corpus.title: Serbian President Vucic Says UN Court ‘Wanted Mladic to Die Behind Bars’
corpus.signal_text:
Serbian President Vucic Says UN Court ‘Wanted Mladic to Die Behind Bars’
This post is also available in this language: Bos/Hrv/Srp
Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic said on Friday that “The Hague wanted [Ratko] Mladic to die behind bars, not in a hospital” because the UN court declined to release the former Bosnian Serb military chief for palliative care in Belgrade ahead of his death.
“We have seen that they did not want to allow the general to die in Serbia, where he wanted to die. That is uncivilised behaviour, behaviour without precedent and without justification,” Vucic said in his first public statement after the death of Mladic on Thursday.
He added that he had been in close contact with Mladic’s family, and that Serbia would ensure that the former Bosnian Serb military leader’s funeral would be “done in a dignified and proper manner”.
On Thursday, Serbia’s Justice Minister Nenad Vujic said that Mladic would be buried with state honours in Serbia. Vucic introduced a note of doubt, however, saying that everything published in the press had been inaccurate.
Vucic also claimed that “the West” had only found Serbs guilty of war crimes from the 1990s.
“Do I believe in justice from The Hague? I never have, and I still do not,” he said.
“All those who took part in crimes against Serbs in the former Yugoslavia were always either acquitted or given token sentences, only for those decisions to later be changed on appeal and the defendants ultimately released,” he added.
Vucic’s statement, slamming the Hague court, echoes Thursday’s reactions to Mladic’s death in pro-government media, among members of the governing Serbian Progressive Party, from hardline nationalist politicians Vojislav Seselj and Aleksandar Vulin and from Bosnian Serb political leader Milorad Dodik.
Serbia is an EU candidate state, and on Friday, the European Commission told Radio Free Europe that it was up to the Belgrade authorities to decide what role they would play in the funeral of convicted war criminal Ratko Mladic.
However, the Commission warned: “The European Commission considers any glorification of war criminals to be contrary to the most fundamental European values and to have no place either in the EU or in countries that are candidates for EU membership.”

corpus.title: IRMCT judge begins investigation into circumstances of Ratko Mladic’s death
corpus.signal_text:
IRMCT judge begins investigation into circumstances of Ratko Mladicâs death
International Residual Mechanism for Criminal Tribunals (IRMCT) Judge Iain Bonomy has arrived in The Hague and begun an investigation into the circumstances surrounding the death of convicted war criminal Ratko Mladic, the Mechanism said Sunday.
Oglas
Bonomy visited the United Nations Detention Unit and the prison hospital where Mladic had been receiving treatment on Saturday, according to the IRMCT.
The investigation remains ongoing, while details are being kept confidential at this stage.
The Mechanism said it remained in regular contact with Mladicâs family, including regarding arrangements for the transfer of his remains.
Dutch authorities confirmed on Saturday that they would not open a criminal investigation into Mladicâs death and that no autopsy would be conducted.
Mladic, the former commander of the Army of Republika Srpska (VRS), died on August 27 in a detention hospital in Scheveningen while serving a life sentence.
He had been in the custody of the UN tribunal system since his arrest in Serbia in 2011, following nearly 16 years on the run.
The former Bosnian Serb military commander was sentenced to life imprisonment after being convicted of genocide in Srebrenica, crimes against humanity and violations of the laws or customs of war committed during the 1992-1995 war in Bosnia and Herzegovina.
Mladic was convicted of genocide for the July 1995 Srebrenica massacre, in which more than 8,000 Bosniak men and boys were killed.
He was also convicted over the campaign of sniping and shelling against civilians during the siege of Sarajevo, persecution and other crimes committed across Bosnia and Herzegovina, as well as the taking of UN personnel hostage.
The International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia (ICTY) convicted Mladic in 2017. His life sentence was upheld on appeal by the IRMCT in 2021.

corpus.title: Ratko Mladić is still viewed as a hero by many Bosnian Serbs. It’s a reminder how divided my country remains today
corpus.signal_text:
I was a 19-year-old living in Banja Luka, the second-largest city in Bosnia, when Yugoslavia began falling apart. What I remember most is the shock and speed with which my normal life and those of my friends abruptly ended.
At the time, I wasn’t following politics or watching the news much, so I had no idea what was to come – a full-blown war and genocide of the Bosniak (Bosnian Muslim people), led by Ratko Mladić, the Bosnian Serbian general and convicted war criminal, who died this week in a prison in The Hague.
Ethnicity was not something my friends and I ever talked about growing up. Two of my best friends were non-Serbs, which I only realised when they suddenly left Bosnia in April and May of 1992.
Soon after, I learned I was to be drafted into the Serbian territorial defence, not knowing what that even was. I went to pick up my uniform and boots, and that’s when my parents put me on the bus to leave the country. I didn’t know where I was going.
This was how I left my country, on my own, for the first time in my life: in haste, without goodbyes, not knowing if or when I would see my family again.
I was not the only one. Almost two million Bosnians were displaced during the war.
Now, with Mladić’s death, these memories of the war are flooding back, juxtaposed with the disheartening scenes of Mladić being celebrated by Serbs in Bosnia as a hero.
He was not a hero; nor is it helpful to refer to him simply as a “madman” or a “butcher”. Mladić is a symbolic reminder of the unresolved legacies of the war – the continued divisions among Bosnians and selective memories that many have about the atrocities that occurred.
Swift rise up the ranks
Mladić was a career military officer in the Yugoslav army. His rise through the ranks was accelerated at the beginning of the Bosnian war when he was named commander-in-chief of the Bosnian Serb army.
It’s important to understand this newly created army inherited all of its armour from the former Yugoslav army. It had all the weapons and military infrastructure in Bosnia, and was led by an experienced professional officer in Mladić.
Mladić’s army quickly took over 70% of the country, laying siege to the capital, Sarajevo. More than 100,000 people died in the war from 1992–95. At least 8,000 Bosniak men and boys were killed by the Bosnian Serb Army in the genocide in Srebrenica in July 1995.
Mladić was the face of this ruthless military campaign, and the rise of Serb nationalism at the time.
